patterns.title: Loans as Cold War reward and punishment
patterns.summary:
US officials used their votes and influence at the IMF, World Bank, Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and the US Export-Import Bank to cut credit to governments they opposed and to open it to governments they backed. The clearest record is Chile. The US Senate Church Committee (1975) found that after Salvador Allende's election in 1970, Washington halted new bilateral aid (NSDM 93, November 1970), Export-Import Bank credits fell to zero in 1971, IDB loans fell from $46 million in 1970 to $2 million in 1972, the World Bank made no new loans from 1970 to 1973, and US short-term commercial credit fell from about $300 million to about $30 million. CIA Director Richard Helms's notes of his 15 September 1970 meeting with President Nixon read "Make the economy scream." Military aid to Chile was not cut. After the September 1973 coup, money returned: a 1978 magazine account put US government aid to the junta at about $350 million, with $125 million committed in 1974 alone.

The same pattern runs through other declassified US records. In Brazil, after the April 1964 coup, the US gave a $50 million AID loan in June 1964, a $150 million program loan in December 1964, and backed a $125 million IMF standby in 1965 (FRUS). In Indonesia, after Suharto displaced Sukarno, the State Department set up a multilateral 'Aid to Indonesia Club' with Japan, the IMF and World Bank (1966), creditors rescheduled over $300 million of arrears (December 1966) and the US committed to one-third of the aid total to support the 'anti-Communist leadership' (FRUS). Allies such as Mobutu's Zaire and Marcos's Philippines kept receiving loans despite known corruption; opponents such as Sandinista Nicaragua saw US 'no' votes at the IDB and World Bank. After the Cold War, debt relief and loans flowed to front-line allies: Egypt after the 1991 Gulf War and Pakistan after September 2001. Peer-reviewed studies support a link but with limits: Thacker (1999, 87 countries, 1985-94) found that moving toward the US in UN votes raised the odds of an IMF loan; Dreher and Jensen (2007, 206 IMF letters of intent, 38 countries, 1997-2003) found close US allies got loans with fewer conditions.

countries.note: The White House, NSC, CIA, Treasury and State Department set lending policy toward Chile (NSDM 93, 1970), Brazil (AID program loans, 1964-66) and Indonesia (one-third aid share, 1966-69), according to the Church Committee report and FRUS documents. The US is the IMF's largest shareholder, which Thacker (1999) and Dreher and Jensen (2007) use to explain their statistical findings.

countries.role: Starved, then rewarded after change of government
countries.note: Under Allende (1970-73), Ex-Im credits fell from $234 million (1967) to zero (1971), IDB loans fell to $2 million in 1972 and the World Bank made no new loans, per the Church Committee. The IMF still extended about $90 million in 1971-72. After the 1973 coup, Moffitt and Letelier (Multinational Monitor, 1978) report about $350 million in US aid, about $400 million from multilateral banks and $380 million from the IMF. In November 1986 the US abstained, rather than voting no, on a World Bank loan to Pinochet's Chile (Christian Science Monitor, 1987).

countries.role: Starved, then rewarded after change of government
countries.note: After the April 1964 coup against Goulart, the US gave a $50 million AID contingency loan (June 1964), a $150 million program loan (December 1964), a $53.6 million Treasury exchange agreement and supported a $125 million IMF standby (1965); Rusk asked Johnson in December 1965 for another $150 million, citing political factors (FRUS 1964-68 vol. XXXI, doc. 224). Toussaint writes that World Bank and IMF loans had been suspended for three years before the coup.

countries.role: Starved, then rewarded after change of government
countries.note: Under Somoza, Nicaragua received nine World Bank loans in 1951-56 and one in 1961, per the Bank's official history as quoted by Toussaint. Under the Sandinistas, the US cast the only 'no' vote on a $16 million World Bank loan (January 1982), vetoed a $2.2 million IDB road loan that 42 other members approved (June 1983), and Nicaragua got no IDB loans in 1984 (Multinational Monitor, 1985). World Bank lending resumed after Violeta Chamorro won the February 1990 election (Toussaint).

countries.role: Starved, then rewarded after change of government
countries.note: The World Bank sent a survey mission in 1951 but made no loan until 1955, after the CIA-backed overthrow of President Arbenz in 1954, according to Toussaint citing the Bank's official history (Kapur, Lewis and Webb, 1997, vol. 1, p. 103).

countries.role: Starved, then rewarded after change of government
countries.note: Michael Manley's government broke off talks with the IMF in March 1980 over a $175 million credit and its budget conditions (Christian Science Monitor, 1980). After Edward Seaga took office in late 1980, the IMF agreed a package of about $650-700 million over three years (April 1981), with $60 million from the US government and a US business committee chaired by David Rockefeller (Christian Science Monitor 1981; Multinational Monitor 1981).

After 1965 the State Department organised a multilateral aid group with Japan, the IMF and World Bank to support Suharto's 'anti-Communist leadership' (FRUS doc. 215, August 1966). Creditors rescheduled over $300 million in arrears (December 1966); donors gave about $200 million in 1967, and the US took one-third, pledging about $123 million of non-food aid for 1969 (FRUS docs. 241 and 1969-76 vol. XX doc. 267).

In June 1981 the IMF approved a three-year loan of about $1.1-1.2 billion to Mobutu's Zaire and 12 Western governments rescheduled about $600 million (Multinational Monitor 1981; Christian Science Monitor 1983). A US Treasury official said withdrawing support from Mobutu would cause 'a breakdown of law and order'. The IMF-commissioned Blumenthal report, leaked in 1982, said creditors had 'no chance' of repayment because of corruption.

World Bank lending to Marcos rose from $30 million to $165 million in 1974, after martial law in 1972, and reached $600 million in 1983, according to Toussaint citing internal Bank memos and the Bank's official history. External debt rose from $2.3 billion (1970) to over $17.2 billion (1980), per the US Library of Congress country study.

After Mubarak joined the US-led Gulf War coalition, the US forgave $7.1 billion of military debt (December 1990), Gulf states forgave about $7 billion, and on 25 May 1991 Paris Club creditors agreed to write off 50% of $20.2 billion; the IMF approved a $372 million standby (Christian Science Monitor, May and July 1991).

After September 2001, the IMF approved a $1.32 billion three-year loan (7 December 2001) and the Paris Club restructured about $12.5 billion (13 December 2001). Dawn (2002) reported $1.5 billion in aid in four months and a $1 billion US package; the World Bank's Islamabad office said the support was based on reforms, not politics.

timeline.event: The World Bank makes its first loan to Guatemala, a year after the 1954 overthrow of President Arbenz; a survey mission in 1951 had led to no loan.
On 12 April the World Bank board approves a loan to Somoza's Nicaragua, five days before the Bay of Pigs invasion launched from Nicaraguan territory.
After the April coup in Brazil, the US gives a $50 million AID contingency loan in June and a $150 million program loan in December.
Brazil's military government gets a $125 million IMF standby and a $53.6 million US Treasury exchange agreement; in December Rusk asks Johnson for another $150 million, citing political factors.
On 4 August Rusk tells Johnson the US and Japan are organising an 'Aid to Indonesia Club' with IMF and World Bank roles to support Indonesia's anti-Communist leadership.
A State Department paper records creditors rescheduling over $300 million of Indonesian arrears (December 1966), $200 million in 1967 aid, and a US pledge of one-third.
Rogers asks Nixon to confirm a US pledge of one-third (about $123 million) of Indonesia's $365 million non-food aid request at the IGGI meeting of 14 April.
Helms's notes of his 15 September meeting with Nixon on Chile read 'Make the economy scream'; NSDM 93 in November halts new bilateral aid.
US Export-Import Bank credits to Chile fall to zero, and a $21 million credit for Boeing jets is deferred in August.
Nixon says in January the US will withhold support from loans under consideration in multilateral banks; IDB loans to Chile fall to $2 million.
The US commits $125 million in aid to Chile's junta in the first full year after the coup, per a 1978 Multinational Monitor account.
World Bank lending to Marcos's Philippines rises from $30 million to $165 million, two years after martial law.
Jamaica's Manley government breaks off IMF talks on a $175 million credit over budget conditions.
Under Seaga, Jamaica agrees an IMF package of close to $700 million over three years, with more from other lenders and banks.
The IMF approves a $1.1 billion three-year loan to Zaire; a US Treasury official cites the risk of disorder if support for Mobutu is withdrawn.
In June the US vetoes a $2.2 million IDB road loan to Nicaragua that the other 42 members approved.
In November the US abstains, after saying it would vote no, on a World Bank loan to Pinochet's Chile.
In December the US forgives $7.1 billion of Egypt's military debt after Egypt joins the Gulf War coalition.
On 25 May Paris Club creditors agree to write off 50% of $20.2 billion owed by Egypt; the IMF approves a $372 million standby.
The IMF approves a $1.32 billion loan to Pakistan on 7 December, and the Paris Club restructures about $12.5 billion on 13 December.

claims_per_author.author: Michael Moffitt and Isabel Letelier
claims_per_author.work: 'Private International Banks Support Chilean Junta', Multinational Monitor, 1978
claims_per_author.claim: Moffitt and Letelier say the junta received about $350 million in US aid, about $400 million from multilateral banks and $380 million from the IMF after 1973, against under $25 million in US aid to Allende over three years.
claims_per_author.status: The Church Committee confirms the cut under Allende but gives no post-coup economic aid totals. Private bank figures came from unnamed 'confidential' sources.

claims_per_author.author: Eric Toussaint (CADTM)
claims_per_author.work: 'Bolsonaro has announced a celebration of the 1964 military coup', Against the Current No. 200, 2019
claims_per_author.claim: Toussaint says World Bank and IMF loans to Brazil had been suspended for three years before the 1964 coup and resumed soon after.
claims_per_author.status: FRUS doc. 224 confirms large US and IMF loans after the coup; the pre-coup suspension is not confirmed in the records consulted.

claims_per_author.author: Eric Toussaint (CADTM)
claims_per_author.work: 'The World Bank and the Philippines', International Viewpoint
claims_per_author.claim: Toussaint says Robert McNamara and Bank staff welcomed Marcos's martial law and raised lending, quoting internal Bank memos of 1972 and 1973.
claims_per_author.status: He cites Kapur, Lewis and Webb, The World Bank: Its First Half Century (1997), vol. 1, pp. 303-304 and 558-565; that volume was not checked directly.

claims_per_author.author: Multinational Monitor (unsigned)
claims_per_author.work: 'Taking Care of Business in Nicaragua', April 1985
claims_per_author.claim: The article lists each US vote against or veto of IDB and World Bank loans to Sandinista Nicaragua in 1981-85.
claims_per_author.status: A single 1985 magazine account; IDB voting records were not checked. Toussaint separately says the World Bank suspended lending over arrears.

uncertain: How much of the World Bank's halt to Chile in 1970-73 came from US pressure and how much from the Bank's own view of Chile's creditworthiness and expropriations is disputed; the Church Committee says the US effort to enlist the banks was only partly successful.
Kedar (2018) finds the World Bank used its claim of economic neutrality to resist US attempts to tie loans to Pinochet to human rights in 1973-77, so the Bank was not always a tool of Washington.

The statistical evidence is mixed in strength: Thacker (1999) found that a country's level of alignment with the US did not reliably predict IMF loans during the Cold War, only movement toward the US did; alignment level mattered in 1990-94.
Dreher and Jensen's finding that close US allies get fewer IMF conditions covers 1997-2003 only and does not show the US directly instructed IMF staff.
For Pakistan in 2001, a World Bank office and an official denied that the US or G-8 pressed the lenders to help because of Musharraf's support for the war in Afghanistan.
The post-coup Chile loan totals and the Nicaragua vote list each rest on one magazine account and need checking against IDB and World Bank board records.
Brazil's treatment before the 1964 coup (whether lending was deliberately withheld from Goulart) is not documented in the records consulted.

patterns.title: Debts run up by dictators, paid by those after them
patterns.summary:
Banks, governments and international lenders lent to dictators who wasted or stole much of the money, and the governments that followed were made to pay it back. In Argentina, external debt rose from $7.5 billion to $43.5 billion under the 1976-1983 junta; on 13 July 2000 federal judge Jorge Ballestero, ruling on a complaint filed by Alejandro Olmos in 1982, found 477 illegal acts and said the IMF, which supervised the talks, could not have failed to notice what was happening. The ruling went to Congress, which only set up a debt monitoring commission in 2014. In the Philippines, the Marcos government borrowed from the US Export-Import Bank to build the $2.3 billion Bataan nuclear plant with Westinghouse; it never produced electricity, and the public finished paying P64.7 billion (P43.5 billion principal, P21.2 billion interest) in April 2007. A Philippine anti-graft court in 2012 ruled that the $50.6 million commission paid to Marcos associate Herminio Disini was ill-gotten.

Peer-reviewed work links such loans to capital flight. Ndikumana and Boyce (1998) found Mobutu's Zaire ran up about $14 billion in public external debt while capital flight reached $12 billion by 1990; their 2008 study of 40 sub-Saharan countries (1970-2004) found that up to 62 cents of each borrowed dollar left the region as capital flight in the same year. In 2004 the Paris Club wrote off 80% of Iraq's $38.9 billion debt from the Saddam era, and the US forgave its full $4.1 billion, but neither used the odious-debt label. Ecuador's 2007-2008 audit commission called much of its debt illegitimate; Ecuador stopped paying $3.2 billion of bonds and in 2009 bought about 91% of them back at 35 cents on the dollar. Norway, on 2 October 2006, cancelled NOK 520 million owed by five countries from its 1976-80 ship export campaign, saying it shared responsibility for a development policy failure.

countries.note: External debt rose from $7.5 billion to $43.5 billion under the 1976-83 junta. Judge Ballestero's 13 July 2000 ruling in the Olmos case found 477 illegal acts and sent the matter to Congress, which created a debt monitoring commission only in 2014 (Law 26.984). A Jubilee 2000 account named Barclays and Lloyds among about 30 British lenders of the period.

An audit commission set up by decree in July 2007 reviewed debts from 1976 to 2007 and in November 2008 called much of the debt illegitimate, accusing Salomon Smith Barney over the 2000 restructuring. Ecuador stopped paying $3.2 billion of 2012 and 2030 bonds and in 2009 repurchased about 91% at 35 cents on the dollar, spending about $900 million. Norway also cancelled NOK 225 million of Ecuador's ship export debt in 2006.

Debt rose from $600 million in 1965 to $26 billion in 1986 (Tadem, Inquirer, 2016). The Bataan plant, financed by the US Export-Import Bank, cost $2.3 billion, never ran, and was fully paid off in April 2007 at P64.7 billion. The Philippines lost its bribery suit against Westinghouse in US court in 1993 and settled with the company for $100 million in October 1995.

Under Mobutu, public external debt reached about $14 billion and capital flight about $12 billion by 1990, nearly $18 billion with interest (Ndikumana and Boyce, 1998). The IMF-commissioned Blumenthal report, leaked in 1982, said creditors had no chance of repayment because of corruption.

Jubilee 2000's South African branch put the apartheid-era debt at R86.7 billion (about $14 billion) in 1993; the post-apartheid government did not seek cancellation, and about 20% of the budget went to debt service in 1999 (The Economist via Probe International; Cape Times). German, Swiss, British, US and French banks were named in a 1999 Jubilee report.

Foreign debt was $750 million when Jean-Claude Duvalier fled in 1986, and more than half of Haiti's debt was contracted under the Duvaliers (1957-86), according to campaign groups. About $1.2 billion was cancelled under the HIPC initiative in 2009. Duvalier assets remained frozen at UBS in Switzerland.

Iraq's public debt was about $120 billion at end-2004. On 21 November 2004 the Paris Club agreed to cut 80% of the $38.9 billion owed to it in three phases tied to an IMF programme, and the US forgave its $4.1 billion on 17 December 2004 (CRS report RS21765).
Norway cancelled NOK 168 million owed by Egypt from the 1976-80 ship export campaign on 2 October 2006.
Norway cancelled NOK 19 million owed by Jamaica from the ship export campaign in 2006.
Norway cancelled NOK 48 million owed by Peru from the ship export campaign in 2006.
Norway cancelled NOK 60 million owed by Sierra Leone from the ship export campaign in 2006; only this part was paid for from Norway's debt relief facility.

On 2 October 2006 Norway cancelled NOK 520 million owed by five countries, calling its 1976-80 ship export campaign a development policy failure for which it shared responsibility. It did not count the cancellation as aid.

The US Export-Import Bank financed the Bataan plant built by Pittsburgh-based Westinghouse. The US forgave all $4.1 billion of Iraq's debt to it in December 2004 at a cost of $360 million to the Treasury (CRS).

timeline.event: Construction of the Bataan nuclear plant begins under Marcos; Westinghouse's first bid was $500 million.
On 4 April journalist Alejandro Olmos files a criminal complaint over Argentina's junta-era foreign debt.
A leaked report by former IMF official Erwin Blumenthal says Zaire's creditors have no chance of repayment because of corruption; debt stands at $4.1 billion.
Argentina's military government leaves office with $43.5 billion in external debt, up from $7.5 billion in 1976.
Corazon Aquino mothballs the $2.3 billion Bataan plant, which never produced electricity.
Jean-Claude Duvalier flees Haiti, leaving $750 million in foreign debt.
Jubilee 2000 South Africa estimates the debt left by the apartheid government at R86.7 billion (about $14 billion).
In October President Ramos signs a $100 million settlement with Westinghouse after the Philippines lost its bribery case in US court.
Ndikumana and Boyce publish estimates that Zaire's public debt reached about $14 billion and capital flight $12 billion by 1990.
On 13 July Judge Jorge Ballestero rules in the Olmos case, finding 477 illegal acts in Argentina's junta-era debt, and refers it to Congress.
On 13 May Jeffrey Winters tells the US Senate that a third of World Bank loan funds to Indonesia were stolen.
On 21 November the Paris Club agrees to cut 80% of Iraq's $38.9 billion debt; on 17 December the US forgives its $4.1 billion.
On 2 October Norway cancels NOK 520 million of ship export debt owed by Ecuador, Egypt, Jamaica, Peru and Sierra Leone.
In April the Philippines finishes paying for the Bataan plant: P64.7 billion, including P21.2 billion in interest.
In July Ecuador's President Correa creates a commission to audit debts contracted from 1976 to 2007.
Ndikumana and Boyce estimate that up to 62 cents of each dollar borrowed by 40 African countries in 1970-2004 left as capital flight.
Ecuador's audit commission calls much of the debt illegitimate and recommends stopping payment on $3.9 billion of global bonds.
Ecuador buys back about 91% of its defaulted 2012 and 2030 bonds at 35 cents on the dollar.
On 11 April the Sandiganbayan rules the $50.6 million Bataan commission paid to Herminio Disini ill-gotten.

claims_per_author.author: Jeffrey Winters
claims_per_author.work: Testimony to the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 13 May 2004
claims_per_author.claim: Winters says a third of World Bank loan funds to Indonesia under Suharto were stolen, and that the Bank took part 'mostly passively' in the corruption of about $100 billion of its loans worldwide.
claims_per_author.status: Winters says the World Bank publicly denied his 1997 allegation and called him irresponsible, and that two leaked internal Bank documents later supported him; those documents were not located.

claims_per_author.author: Erwin Blumenthal
claims_per_author.work: Report on Zaire for the IMF, leaked 1982 (as reported by the Christian Science Monitor)
claims_per_author.claim: Blumenthal says corruption by Mobutu's ruling group made repayment impossible; press accounts of the report put Mobutu's fortune at $4-5 billion.
claims_per_author.status: The report itself was not found online. Austrian MPs in a 1998-99 parliamentary question said the report was suppressed and aid to Zaire increased afterward, without giving figures.

claims_per_author.author: Michael Kremer (as cited by Upside Down World)
claims_per_author.work: Cited in 'IDB Debt Cancellation for Haiti', 2006
claims_per_author.claim: Kremer reports that Jean-Claude Duvalier stole $900 million.
claims_per_author.status: Toussaint and Perchellet (2010) cite a similar $900 million figure for the family's bank holdings; no court finding or official audit of the sum was found.

claims_per_author.author: Eduardo C. Tadem
claims_per_author.claim: Tadem says Philippine external debt rose from $600 million in 1965 to $26 billion in 1986.
claims_per_author.status: The Library of Congress country study confirms a rise from $2.3 billion (1970) to over $17.2 billion (1980) but gives no 1986 total.

uncertain: 'Odious debt' is not an established rule of international law; the CRS report on Iraq says so, and creditors cut Iraq's debt through the normal Paris Club process tied to IMF conditions, not by accepting that the debt was odious.
Norway's 2006 statement does not use the words 'odious' or 'illegitimate'; it speaks of a development policy failure and shared responsibility.
Westinghouse said it paid Disini only $17 million and called it a legitimate sales commission; a New Jersey jury acquitted Westinghouse and Burns and Roe of bribery in 1993.
Ecuador's default was a suspension based on its own audit; creditors and rating agencies treated it as a default, and no court has ruled the bonds illegitimate.
The Olmos ruling found illegal acts but led to no conviction and no change to Argentina's repayment of the debt.

South Africa's 'apartheid debt' figure of R86.7 billion comes from Jubilee 2000 and includes liabilities not usually counted as sovereign debt; the finance ministry said only R240 million in foreign apartheid-era debt was outstanding in 1999.
Haiti figures on the Duvalier share of debt and the stolen sum come from campaign groups (CADTM, Jubilee) citing an IMF report; the IMF document was not checked directly.
Ndikumana and Boyce's capital flight estimates are calculated as residuals from balance-of-payments data and show association between borrowing and flight, not that each loan was stolen.
